cells.tense: You are reading the whole of it, and the read keeps opening instead of closing.
cells.ask: Take one thing you see clearly and work it one more day. No push to finish. Notice whether it still has something to teach you.
cells.core:
You can step back far enough to see how the pieces fit and still keep your hands on the work. That's harder than it sounds.

Nothing you see has to be final for it to be true. In the corner where you practice, that looks like one more pass without needing to be done — patient, unhurried, still asking. You get to keep going without settling it.

The risk on the other side is staying open until it slides into staying loose. So stay near the people your read touches. When something lands, say it out loud to someone who'll bring their own read back. A short back-and-forth, no verdict. That keeps a clear eye from going cold.

cells.tense: You will keep holding every piece up against a bar you move before you reach it.
cells.ask: Pick one person or one piece of work and make a single clear call about it this week. Hold that call seven days without re-grading it. Revise after, not during.
cells.core:
You can see how the thing should go, and lately you look at it more coldly than you mean to. From 'here's what's off' it's one short step to 'and that's the problem with them' — and the step keeps taking itself.

In practice that shows up as standing over your own shoulder, correcting before the rep is finished. You're not reading more than before; you've just moved your eye further up from the work. The distance you use to see the whole thing has quietly become the distance you hold everything at.

The way back is a choice, not more analysis. Choose one thing you're willing to be wrong about and serve it plainly for a week: one student, one page, one detail. No grade attached. Serve it plain and it stops being a verdict.

cells.tense: You came up to the edge of starting and you have not walked in yet.
cells.ask: Do the crudest version of one practice you've been circling — a beginner's first step, badly, small, for a few minutes today. No plan for tomorrow.
cells.core:
You've read about the practice more than you've sat down inside it. The real version keeps waiting for the next one — the better setup, the right week — and today's small version goes untouched.

What's hard here isn't seeing. You see fine. What's hard is landing it — turning what you notice into a repetition your hands can do. More willpower won't fix that. A first move too small to count as a serious attempt will.

Sit with the thing you've been reading about and do the rough draft of it. Not polished, not planned. A few minutes, clumsy, real. That's what starts the practice instead of continuing the study of it.

cells.tense: You are reading the room right now while calling it nothing special to notice.
cells.ask: When the next clear read comes, say it as yours — 'here's what I see' — and drop the 'anyone would notice that.' Saying so out loud is the practice.
cells.core:
The reading is running. You catch how a piece fits before anyone says it, you feel where a session is heading before the reps prove it. Then you wave it off — obvious, anyone would see that.

So the read happens and nobody can tell whose it is. Treated as the room's read instead of yours, it leaves you with no way of knowing how much of what moves here comes from you.

What brings it back is simpler than the read itself: fair accounting. In your corner, keep track of the small calls you make — what you noticed, what you chose to repeat, what you dropped. Then when the next clear read lands, put your name on it.

attempts.check: Unsupported claim: 'the room where saying it didn't go well' in Too Little — the record locates the person at a door but never says a bad room stood behind it, so I kept the cost of holding back unnamed. Reader's likely objection: that Too Much's hardness is really just high standards, not looking down at anyone — the mechanism doesn't need their motive, and the copy describes the sorting gone stiff, which they can deny and still use. The ask survives a wrong read in every cell because the act itself teaches something: one clean cut, one badly-worded sentence, one unedited block, one plain-credit sentence. Sentence serving the writer, cut: 'and you'd be right about most of it' — it flatters the writer's own cleverness about them, not the person.
